title: CTS Parables of the Bible — Unit 8: The Kingdom Parables

blocks.en: 🌱 Parables of the Bible — Unit 8: The Kingdom Parables
blocks.es_reference: 🌱 Las Parábolas de la Biblia — Unidad 8: Las Parábolas del Reino

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field." — Matthew 13:31 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "El reino de los cielos es semejante al grano de mostaza, que un hombre tomó y sembró en su campo." — Mateo 13:31 (RVG)

blocks.en: Orientation
blocks.es_reference: Orientación

blocks.en: In Unit 7 we studied the parable of the sower, the parable that teaches us how to hear all the others. Matthew 13 places the sower first in a collection of seven parables about the kingdom of heaven, and then adds six more: the wheat and the tares, the mustard seed, the leaven, the hidden treasure, the pearl of great price, and the dragnet. Matthew arranges them carefully. The chapter comes right after the religious leaders accused Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebub (Matthew 12:24), and from this point Jesus begins teaching the crowds in parables.
blocks.es_reference: En la Unidad 7 estudiamos la parábola del sembrador, la parábola que nos enseña a oír todas las demás. Mateo 13 coloca al sembrador en primer lugar en una colección de siete parábolas acerca del reino de los cielos, y luego añade seis más: el trigo y la cizaña, el grano de mostaza, la levadura, el tesoro escondido, la perla preciosa y la red. Mateo las ordena con cuidado. El capítulo viene justo después de que los líderes religiosos acusaron a Jesús de echar fuera demonios por Beelzebú (Mateo 12:24), y desde ese momento Jesús comienza a enseñar a las multitudes en parábolas.

blocks.en: These parables answer questions Jesus' followers were surely asking. If the kingdom of God has really come, why is evil still growing alongside good? Why does the kingdom look so small? And is it worth the cost of following Jesus? The answers are simple and profound: the kingdom grows mixed with evil until the harvest; it begins small but becomes great; and it is worth everything we have.
blocks.es_reference: Estas parábolas responden preguntas que sin duda se hacían los seguidores de Jesús. Si el reino de Dios realmente ha llegado, ¿por qué el mal sigue creciendo junto al bien? ¿Por qué el reino se ve tan pequeño? ¿Y vale la pena el costo de seguir a Jesús? Las respuestas son sencillas y profundas: el reino crece mezclado con el mal hasta la siega; comienza pequeño pero llega a ser grande; y vale todo lo que tenemos.

blocks.en: I. The Wheat and the Tares: Growing Together Until the Harvest (Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43)
blocks.es_reference: I. El trigo y la cizaña: crecer juntos hasta la siega (Mateo 13:24–30, 36–43)

blocks.en: A farmer sowed good seed in his field, "but while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat and went his way" (13:25). The tare was probably bearded darnel, a weed that looks almost exactly like wheat until the heads form. When the servants discovered it, they asked whether they should pull it up. "No," the master said, "lest while you gather up the tares you also uproot the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest" (13:29–30). At harvest time the darnel would be separated and burned.
blocks.es_reference: Un agricultor sembró buena semilla en su campo, "pero mientras dormían los hombres, vino su enemigo y sembró cizaña entre el trigo, y se fue" (13:25). La cizaña probablemente era la cizaña barbada, una maleza que se parece casi exactamente al trigo hasta que se forman las espigas. Cuando los siervos la descubrieron, preguntaron si debían arrancarla. "No", dijo el amo, "no sea que al arrancar la cizaña, arranquéis también con ella el trigo. Dejad crecer juntamente lo uno y lo otro hasta la siega" (13:29–30). En el tiempo de la siega la cizaña sería separada y quemada.

blocks.en: Jesus explains that He is the sower, "the field is the world, the good seeds are the sons of the kingdom, but the tares are the sons of the wicked one," the enemy is the devil, and the harvest is the end of the age (13:37–39). Evil has not been driven out of one town or even one home on earth. Even among Jesus' twelve, one denied Him and another betrayed Him.
blocks.es_reference: Jesús explica que Él es el sembrador, que "el campo es el mundo; la buena semilla son los hijos del reino, y la cizaña son los hijos del malo", que el enemigo es el diablo y que la siega es el fin del siglo (13:37–39). El mal no ha sido expulsado de un solo pueblo ni siquiera de un solo hogar en la tierra. Aun entre los doce de Jesús, uno lo negó y otro lo traicionó.

blocks.en: Careful students should notice an interpretive question. Jesus says the field is the world, not the church, and the parable teaches that God will not separate the righteous from the wicked in this age. In church history the parable was sometimes used to argue that the church should never discipline its members. Most interpreters answer that other passages clearly call for church discipline (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5), so this parable is not a ban on correction. It is a warning against trying to do what only God can do: to judge hearts and make the final separation. A tare can only be recognized by one who looks on the inside. When I was a boy hoeing corn, I would sometimes find a weed growing right next to a stalk. Trying to cut the weed, how many times I cut the corn too!
blocks.es_reference: Los estudiantes cuidadosos deben notar una pregunta de interpretación. Jesús dice que el campo es el mundo, no la iglesia, y la parábola enseña que Dios no separará a los justos de los malos en este siglo. En la historia de la iglesia a veces se usó la parábola para argumentar que la iglesia nunca debía disciplinar a sus miembros. La mayoría de los intérpretes responden que otros pasajes claramente piden disciplina en la iglesia (Mateo 18:15–17; 1 Corintios 5), así que esta parábola no prohíbe la corrección. Es una advertencia contra intentar hacer lo que solo Dios puede hacer: juzgar los corazones y hacer la separación final. La cizaña solo puede reconocerla quien mira por dentro. Cuando yo era niño y escardaba maíz, a veces encontraba una maleza creciendo pegada a una mata. ¡Cuántas veces, al tratar de cortar la maleza, corté también el maíz!

blocks.en: The weeds grow not only in the world but inside the church and inside each heart. A woman on a television talk show once explained that she had carried on a long affair with a married man. When someone raised the question of morality, she protested, "I am a Christian, but my personal life and my religion don't have anything to do with one another. God wants me to be happy." Tares can speak the language of wheat. And yet the opposite is also true. When Jesus met the woman at the well in Samaria, a seemingly hopeless wreck of a life, He saw something growing in her: a longing for living water, like a little stalk of wheat struggling for life among the weeds (John 4). Only God sees the heart clearly. I used to think I could tell an honest man from a dishonest one, but after years of lending small sums to strangers and almost never being repaid, I have learned that my judgment is not as accurate as I thought. The Devil can make his tares look so much like wheat that they sometimes look better than the wheat. They just do not make very good bread.
blocks.es_reference: La cizaña no crece solo en el mundo, sino también dentro de la iglesia y dentro de cada corazón. Una mujer en un programa de televisión explicó una vez que había tenido un largo amorío con un hombre casado. Cuando alguien planteó la cuestión moral, ella protestó: "Soy cristiana, pero mi vida personal y mi religión no tienen nada que ver una con la otra. Dios quiere que yo sea feliz." La cizaña puede hablar el idioma del trigo. Y sin embargo, lo contrario también es cierto. Cuando Jesús conoció a la mujer samaritana junto al pozo, una vida que parecía un naufragio sin esperanza, vio algo que crecía en ella: un anhelo del agua viva, como una pequeña espiga de trigo que lucha por vivir entre la maleza (Juan 4). Solo Dios ve el corazón con claridad. Yo antes pensaba que podía distinguir a un hombre honrado de uno deshonesto, pero después de años de prestar pequeñas cantidades a desconocidos y casi nunca recibir el pago, he aprendido que mi juicio no es tan certero como pensaba. El diablo puede hacer que su cizaña se parezca tanto al trigo que a veces se ve mejor que el trigo. Solo que no hace muy buen pan.

blocks.en: The parable also carries a solemn warning. Tares may attend church, teach, and pray in public. But the harvest will reveal them. "Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of My Father in heaven" (Matthew 7:21). A counterfeit bill may pass from hand to hand and buy many things, but when it reaches the bank, it is exposed and taken out of circulation. There is an old legend of a man in ancient China who got a place in the emperor's orchestra by pretending to play the flute. When the emperor announced that every musician would play a solo, the man could not face the music. Pretending may last a long time, but it will not last forever.
blocks.es_reference: La parábola también lleva una advertencia solemne. La cizaña puede asistir a la iglesia, enseñar y orar en público. Pero la siega la revelará. "No todo el que me dice: Señor, Señor, entrará en el reino de los cielos, sino el que hace la voluntad de mi Padre que está en los cielos" (Mateo 7:21). Un billete falso puede pasar de mano en mano y comprar muchas cosas, pero cuando llega al banco, queda expuesto y lo sacan de circulación. Hay una antigua leyenda de un hombre en la China antigua que consiguió un lugar en la orquesta del emperador fingiendo tocar la flauta. Cuando el emperador anunció que cada músico tocaría un solo, el hombre no pudo enfrentar la música. El fingimiento puede durar mucho tiempo, pero no durará para siempre.

blocks.en: So the question is personal: am I wheat? The answer is not found by comparing ourselves with others but by turning to Christ: "Whoever calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved" (Romans 10:13). Remember too that whatever we sow, we will reap. A Salvation Army paper once told of a bitter tenant farmer who learned he was losing his lease. In anger, he scattered the seeds of the worst weeds he could find all over the clean fields. The next morning the owner told him the plans had changed and he could renew his lease after all. "Oh, Lord," he cried, "what a fool I've been!" He would spend years pulling up the weeds he had sown himself.
blocks.es_reference: Así que la pregunta es personal: ¿soy trigo? La respuesta no se encuentra comparándonos con otros, sino volviéndonos a Cristo: "todo aquel que invocare el nombre del Señor, será salvo" (Romanos 10:13). Recuerde también que todo lo que sembramos, eso segaremos. Un periódico del Ejército de Salvación contó una vez de un arrendatario amargado que supo que perdería su contrato. Con enojo, esparció las semillas de las peores malezas que pudo encontrar por todos los campos limpios. A la mañana siguiente el dueño le dijo que los planes habían cambiado y que después de todo podía renovar su contrato. "¡Oh, Señor", clamó, "qué necio he sido!" Pasaría años arrancando la maleza que él mismo había sembrado.

blocks.en: II. The Mustard Seed: Small Beginnings (Matthew 13:31–32)
blocks.es_reference: II. El grano de mostaza: comienzos pequeños (Mateo 13:31–32)

blocks.en: "The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field, which indeed is the least of all the seeds; but when it is grown it is greater than the herbs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches" (13:31–32). Mustard greens are a favorite dish in Louisiana, but the kind grown in Galilee, black mustard, could grow taller than a man in a single season, from a seed so small it was proverbial. Jesus was not giving a botany lesson on the smallest seed in the world; He used the proverbial smallest seed His hearers knew.
blocks.es_reference: "El reino de los cielos es semejante al grano de mostaza, que un hombre tomó y sembró en su campo; el cual a la verdad es la más pequeña de todas las semillas; pero cuando ha crecido, es la mayor de las hortalizas, y se hace árbol, de tal manera que vienen las aves del cielo y hacen nidos en sus ramas" (13:31–32). Las hojas de mostaza son un platillo favorito en Luisiana, pero la clase que se cultivaba en Galilea, la mostaza negra, podía crecer más alta que un hombre en una sola temporada, a partir de una semilla tan pequeña que era proverbial. Jesús no daba una clase de botánica sobre la semilla más pequeña del mundo; usaba la semilla proverbialmente más pequeña que conocían Sus oyentes.

blocks.en: The image of a great tree with birds nesting in its branches comes from the Old Testament, where it pictures a great kingdom sheltering the nations (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12). Jesus' kingdom began with a carpenter from Nazareth and twelve ordinary men. Today it has spread to every continent. Most interpreters read the parable as a promise of astonishing growth. Some, especially in older dispensational teaching, read the birds as evil and the unusual growth as the corruption of the church. The larger context of hopeful growth parables supports the positive reading, but students should know both views.
blocks.es_reference: La imagen de un gran árbol con aves que anidan en sus ramas viene del Antiguo Testamento, donde representa un gran reino que da refugio a las naciones (Ezequiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12). El reino de Jesús comenzó con un carpintero de Nazaret y doce hombres comunes. Hoy se ha extendido a todos los continentes. La mayoría de los intérpretes leen la parábola como una promesa de crecimiento asombroso. Algunos, especialmente en la enseñanza dispensacionalista antigua, leen las aves como el mal y el crecimiento inusual como la corrupción de la iglesia. El contexto más amplio de parábolas de crecimiento esperanzador apoya la lectura positiva, pero los estudiantes deben conocer ambas posturas.

blocks.en: Jesus used the mustard seed a second time to speak of faith: "if you have faith as a mustard seed... nothing will be impossible for you" (Matthew 17:20). As my seminary student told us in Unit 7, "I only began with a mustard seed of faith, but it grew." God does not require great faith to begin. He requires real faith, planted in good soil, and He gives the growth.
blocks.es_reference: Jesús usó el grano de mostaza por segunda vez para hablar de la fe: "si tuviereis fe como un grano de mostaza... nada os será imposible" (Mateo 17:20). Como nos contó mi estudiante del seminario en la Unidad 7: "Solo comencé con un grano de mostaza de fe, pero creció." Dios no exige una gran fe para comenzar. Exige una fe real, sembrada en buena tierra, y Él da el crecimiento.

blocks.en: III. The Leaven: Hidden Power (Matthew 13:33)
blocks.es_reference: III. La levadura: un poder escondido (Mateo 13:33)

blocks.en: "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal till it was all leavened" (13:33). The leaven Jesus described was not packaged yeast but a piece of fermented dough saved from the last baking, the way many cooks still keep a sourdough starter. Three measures of meal was an enormous amount, roughly fifty pounds of flour, enough to make bread for a hundred people or more. It is the same amount Sarah baked when the Lord visited Abraham (Genesis 18:6). A small piece of leaven, worked into that great mass of dough, quietly spread until every part of it rose.
blocks.es_reference: "El reino de los cielos es semejante a la levadura que tomó una mujer, y escondió en tres medidas de harina, hasta que todo fue leudado" (13:33). La levadura que Jesús describió no era levadura empacada, sino un pedazo de masa fermentada guardado de la horneada anterior, como muchas cocineras todavía guardan una masa madre. Tres medidas de harina eran una cantidad enorme, unos veinte kilos de harina, suficiente para hacer pan para cien personas o más. Es la misma cantidad que Sara horneó cuando el Señor visitó a Abraham (Génesis 18:6). Un pequeño pedazo de levadura, trabajado en esa gran masa, se extendió calladamente hasta que toda ella se levantó.

blocks.en: Leaven usually pictures sin or corruption elsewhere in Scripture: "Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees" (Matthew 16:6), and "a little leaven leavens the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6). A few interpreters therefore read this parable as a warning that false teaching would spread through the church. Most interpreters, however, note that Jesus explicitly says the kingdom of heaven is like the leaven, and that the parable is paired with the mustard seed, a picture of growth. They conclude that Jesus deliberately used a surprising image to teach that the kingdom works quietly, from the inside out, until it transforms everything it touches. The mustard seed shows the kingdom's outward growth; the leaven shows its inward power. The gospel does not usually change a society by force from the outside. It changes people from within, one heart at a time, until whole families, towns, and cultures are different.
blocks.es_reference: En otras partes de la Escritura la levadura suele representar el pecado o la corrupción: "Guardaos de la levadura de los fariseos" (Mateo 16:6), y "un poco de levadura leuda toda la masa" (1 Corintios 5:6). Por eso algunos intérpretes leen esta parábola como una advertencia de que la falsa enseñanza se extendería por la iglesia. La mayoría de los intérpretes, sin embargo, notan que Jesús dice expresamente que el reino de los cielos es semejante a la levadura, y que la parábola va junto al grano de mostaza, un cuadro de crecimiento. Concluyen que Jesús usó a propósito una imagen sorprendente para enseñar que el reino obra calladamente, de adentro hacia afuera, hasta transformar todo lo que toca. El grano de mostaza muestra el crecimiento exterior del reino; la levadura muestra su poder interior. El evangelio no suele cambiar una sociedad por la fuerza desde fuera. Cambia a las personas desde dentro, un corazón a la vez, hasta que familias, pueblos y culturas enteras son diferentes.

blocks.en: IV. The Hidden Treasure and the Pearl: Worth Everything (Matthew 13:44–46)
blocks.es_reference: IV. El tesoro escondido y la perla: vale todo (Mateo 13:44–46)

blocks.en: A man found treasure hidden in a field, "and for joy over it he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field" (13:44). A merchant searching for fine pearls found "one pearl of great price" and "went and sold all that he had and bought it" (13:46). In a land often crossed by armies, people really did bury their valuables, and sometimes they never returned. One man stumbles on the kingdom by surprise; the other finds it after a long search. Both respond the same way: they give up everything, and they do it with joy.
blocks.es_reference: Un hombre halló un tesoro escondido en un campo, "y gozoso por ello va y vende todo lo que tiene, y compra aquel campo" (13:44). Un mercader que buscaba buenas perlas halló "una perla preciosa" y "fue y vendió todo lo que tenía, y la compró" (13:46). En una tierra atravesada a menudo por ejércitos, la gente de verdad enterraba sus objetos de valor, y a veces nunca regresaba. Un hombre se topa con el reino por sorpresa; el otro lo encuentra después de una larga búsqueda. Ambos responden igual: renuncian a todo, y lo hacen con gozo.

blocks.en: These parables are the opposite of the thorny ground and the rich young ruler. The young ruler would not sell what he had, and he went away sad. The man in the field sold everything and went away glad. The young woman in West Africa who sold her life for a single coin to lay at Jesus' feet understood the pearl of great price. The kingdom costs everything, and it is worth far more than it costs.
blocks.es_reference: Estas parábolas son lo opuesto al terreno de espinos y al joven rico. El joven rico no quiso vender lo que tenía, y se fue triste. El hombre del campo vendió todo y se fue gozoso. La joven de África Occidental que vendió su vida por una sola moneda para ponerla a los pies de Jesús entendió la perla preciosa. El reino cuesta todo, y vale mucho más de lo que cuesta.

blocks.en: Some readers ask whether the man in the field acted honestly by buying the land without telling the owner about the treasure. Jewish law of the time had rules about found property, and interpreters discuss them, but the parable is not teaching real estate ethics. It uses an everyday situation to make one point: when you discover something of infinite worth, you gladly give up everything else to have it. Another group of interpreters reads the pearl merchant as Christ Himself, who gave up everything to purchase His church. That reading teaches a true doctrine, but most interpreters believe the parallel with the treasure in the field points to the person who finds the kingdom. The missionary Jim Elliot, who was killed in 1956 while trying to reach the Waorani people of Ecuador, had written years earlier in his journal: "He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose." He understood the pearl of great price.
blocks.es_reference: Algunos lectores preguntan si el hombre del campo actuó con honestidad al comprar el terreno sin decirle al dueño lo del tesoro. La ley judía de la época tenía reglas sobre los objetos hallados, y los intérpretes las discuten, pero la parábola no enseña ética de bienes raíces. Usa una situación cotidiana para enseñar un solo punto: cuando uno descubre algo de valor infinito, con gusto renuncia a todo lo demás para tenerlo. Otro grupo de intérpretes lee al mercader de perlas como Cristo mismo, que renunció a todo para comprar a Su iglesia. Esa lectura enseña una doctrina verdadera, pero la mayoría de los intérpretes creen que el paralelo con el tesoro en el campo señala a la persona que encuentra el reino. El misionero Jim Elliot, asesinado en 1956 mientras intentaba alcanzar al pueblo waorani del Ecuador, había escrito años antes en su diario: "No es necio el que da lo que no puede retener para ganar lo que no puede perder." Él entendió la perla preciosa.

blocks.en: V. The Dragnet and the Householder (Matthew 13:47–52)
blocks.es_reference: V. La red y el padre de familia (Mateo 13:47–52)

blocks.en: The collection closes with a parable from the Sea of Galilee itself. "The kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet that was cast into the sea and gathered some of every kind, which, when it was full, they drew to shore; and they sat down and gathered the good into vessels, but threw the bad away" (13:47–48). A dragnet was a long net weighted at the bottom and pulled between two boats or dragged to shore, catching everything in its path. Only on the beach were the fish sorted. Jesus explains that the sorting pictures the end of the age, when the angels will separate the wicked from the just (13:49–50). Like the wheat and the tares, the dragnet teaches that the final separation belongs to God and comes at the end. Our task is to cast the net wide.
blocks.es_reference: La colección termina con una parábola tomada del mismo mar de Galilea. "El reino de los cielos es semejante a una red, que echada en el mar, recoge de toda clase de peces; y una vez llena, la sacan a la orilla; y sentados, recogen lo bueno en cestas, y lo malo echan fuera" (13:47–48). La red barredera era una red larga con pesas en la parte de abajo que se jalaba entre dos barcas o se arrastraba hasta la orilla, atrapando todo lo que encontraba a su paso. Solo en la playa se separaban los peces. Jesús explica que la separación representa el fin del siglo, cuando los ángeles apartarán a los malos de entre los justos (13:49–50). Como el trigo y la cizaña, la red enseña que la separación final le pertenece a Dios y viene al final. Nuestra tarea es echar la red a lo ancho.

blocks.en: Then Jesus asked His disciples, "Have you understood all these things?" They said, "Yes, Lord." And He said, "Therefore every scribe instructed concerning the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old" (13:51–52). This last little parable is a word for every preacher and teacher. The one who understands the kingdom has a storehouse. He brings out the old treasures of the Law and the Prophets and the new treasures of Christ's teaching, and he serves them together. A faithful pastor does not throw away the old for the sake of novelty, nor refuse the new light Christ brings. He brings out both.
blocks.es_reference: Luego Jesús preguntó a Sus discípulos: "¿Habéis entendido todas estas cosas?" Ellos dijeron: "Sí, Señor." Y Él les dijo: "Por eso todo escriba docto en el reino de los cielos es semejante a un padre de familia, que saca de su tesoro cosas nuevas y cosas viejas" (13:51–52). Esta última pequeña parábola es una palabra para todo predicador y maestro. El que entiende el reino tiene un almacén. Saca los tesoros viejos de la Ley y los Profetas y los tesoros nuevos de la enseñanza de Cristo, y los sirve juntos. Un pastor fiel no desecha lo viejo por amor a la novedad, ni rechaza la nueva luz que Cristo trae. Saca ambos.

blocks.en: VI. Preaching the Kingdom Parables
blocks.es_reference: VI. Cómo predicar las parábolas del reino

blocks.en: The wheat and the tares can be preached in movements: the sowing, the growing together, and the harvest, when God will separate. Close with the personal question, "Am I wheat?" and the invitation of Romans 10:13. The mustard seed and the leaven belong together as a sermon of encouragement for small churches and discouraged believers: the kingdom's outward growth and its inward power. The treasure and the pearl call for total commitment with joy, and they preach well beside the rich young ruler, who would not sell what he had. The dragnet can close a series with the certainty of the final judgment and the urgency of casting the net. And the householder reminds the preacher to bring out treasures both new and old. Taken together, Matthew 13 tells the whole story of the kingdom: it grows mixed with evil, starts small and becomes great, works from the inside out, is worth everything, and ends in a harvest.
blocks.es_reference: El trigo y la cizaña pueden predicarse en movimientos: la siembra, el crecer juntos y la siega, cuando Dios separará. Concluya con la pregunta personal: "¿Soy trigo?" y la invitación de Romanos 10:13. El grano de mostaza y la levadura van juntos como un sermón de ánimo para iglesias pequeñas y creyentes desanimados: el crecimiento exterior del reino y su poder interior. El tesoro y la perla llaman a un compromiso total con gozo, y se predican bien junto al joven rico, que no quiso vender lo que tenía. La red puede cerrar una serie con la certeza del juicio final y la urgencia de echar la red. Y el padre de familia recuerda al predicador sacar tesoros nuevos y viejos. Juntas, las parábolas de Mateo 13 cuentan toda la historia del reino: crece mezclado con el mal, comienza pequeño y llega a ser grande, obra de adentro hacia afuera, vale todo y termina en una siega.

blocks.en: Closing
blocks.es_reference: Conclusión

blocks.en: A tiny seed becomes a great tree. A pinch of leaven raises a mountain of dough. A treasure hidden in a field is worth everything a man owns. That is the kingdom of heaven. It does not look impressive at first, and it grows alongside weeds that sometimes look better than the wheat. But the harvest is coming, and on that day every counterfeit will be exposed and every faithful seed will bear its full fruit. The only question that matters is whether we have found the treasure, and whether, with joy, we have given everything to have it.
blocks.es_reference: Una semilla diminuta se convierte en un gran árbol. Un poco de levadura levanta una montaña de masa. Un tesoro escondido en un campo vale todo lo que un hombre posee. Así es el reino de los cielos. Al principio no parece impresionante, y crece junto a una maleza que a veces se ve mejor que el trigo. Pero la siega viene, y en ese día todo lo falso será expuesto y toda semilla fiel dará su fruto completo. La única pregunta que importa es si hemos encontrado el tesoro, y si, con gozo, hemos dado todo por tenerlo.

mc.stem: The tares in Matthew 13 were probably darnel, which:
options: Looks almost exactly like wheat until the heads form
mc.why: That is why the servants could not safely pull it up.

mc.stem: Why did the master tell the servants not to pull up the tares?
options: The tares would turn into wheat
They might uproot the wheat with them
mc.why: "Let both grow together until the harvest" (Matthew 13:30).

mc.stem: In Jesus' explanation, the field in the parable of the wheat and tares is:
mc.why: "The field is the world" (Matthew 13:38), so the parable is not a ban on church discipline.

mc.stem: The illustration of hoeing corn warns that:
options: Trying to root out weeds ourselves can harm the good plants
mc.why: Judging hearts and making the final separation belongs to God alone.

mc.stem: The counterfeit bill and the legend of the flute player illustrate that:
options: Pretending may last a long time but will be exposed
mc.why: "Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' shall enter the kingdom" (Matthew 7:21).

mc.stem: The bitter tenant farmer who scattered weed seeds illustrates that:
options: Whatever we sow, we will reap
mc.why: He kept the farm after all and had to live with the weeds he had sown.

mc.stem: Why does this unit say Jesus called the mustard seed "the least of all the seeds"?
options: He used the proverbially smallest seed His hearers knew, not a botany lesson
It is the smallest seed on earth
mc.why: Galilean black mustard grew from a tiny seed to a plant taller than a man.

mc.stem: The image of birds nesting in a great tree comes from Old Testament passages that picture:
options: A great kingdom sheltering the nations
mc.why: See Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12. Most read the parable as a promise of growth.

mc.stem: The parable of the leaven (Matthew 13:33) teaches that the kingdom:
options: Grows quietly from the inside out until it fills everything
mc.why: Leaven usually pictures sin, but most interpreters see an unexpected image of hidden, unstoppable growth here.

mc.stem: How did the man with the hidden treasure and the pearl merchant respond?
options: They kept the discovery secret and left
They sold only part of what they had
They sold all they had, with joy
mc.why: Unlike the rich young ruler, they gave everything and went away glad.

mc.stem: Taken together, the parables of Mark 4 and Matthew 13 teach that the kingdom:
options: Is received the same way by everyone
Is received differently, grows mixed with evil, starts small, and is worth everything
mc.why: The chapter tells the whole story of the kingdom from sowing to harvest.

mc.stem: Matthew 13 contains how many parables about the kingdom of heaven?
mc.why: The sower, wheat and tares, mustard seed, leaven, hidden treasure, pearl, and dragnet.

mc.stem: The woman at the well illustrates that:
options: Jesus could see wheat struggling to grow in a heart full of weeds
Only religious people have wheat in them
mc.why: Only God sees the heart clearly (John 4).

mc.stem: The leaven in Jesus' parable was probably:
options: A piece of fermented dough saved from the last baking
mc.why: Like a sourdough starter, it spread through the whole batch.

mc.stem: "Three measures of meal" was:
options: An enormous amount, about fifty pounds of flour, the same Sarah baked in Genesis 18:6
mc.why: Enough to make bread for a hundred people or more.

mc.stem: According to this unit, the mustard seed and the leaven together show the kingdom's:
mc.why: The gospel changes people from within, one heart at a time.

mc.stem: Jim Elliot's statement "He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose" illustrates:
mc.why: Elliot gave his life trying to reach the Waorani of Ecuador.

mc.stem: A dragnet sorted the fish:
options: Only on the shore, after it was full
mc.why: The sorting pictures the end of the age when angels separate the wicked from the just.

mc.stem: The householder who brings out "things new and old" (13:52) is a picture of:
options: The teacher of the kingdom who serves both the Old Testament and Christ's teaching
mc.why: A faithful pastor neither throws away the old nor refuses the new.

mc.stem: Some interpreters read the pearl merchant as:
options: Christ, who gave up everything to purchase His church
mc.why: Most, however, see the parallel with the treasure as pointing to the one who finds the kingdom.

fill.prompt: "While men ____, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat."
Mustard greens are a favorite dish in ____.
A woman hid a little ____ in flour till it was all leavened.
The merchant found one ____ of great price and sold all he had to buy it.
Matthew 13 gathers ____ parables about the kingdom of heaven.
The woman hid the leaven in three ____ of meal.
A dragnet gathered fish of every ____.
The householder brings out of his treasure things new and ____.

sa.prompt: Retell the parable of the wheat and tares and give Jesus' explanation of it.
sa.model: While men slept, an enemy sowed tares, probably darnel, among the wheat; it looked like wheat until the heads formed. The master told the servants not to pull it up, lest they uproot the wheat, but to let both grow together until the harvest. Jesus explained that He is the sower, the field is the world, the good seed are the sons of the kingdom, the tares are the sons of the wicked one, the enemy is the devil, and the harvest is the end of the age.

sa.prompt: Explain the interpretive question about church discipline in the wheat and tares, and the warning the parable carries.
sa.model: Jesus says the field is the world, not the church, so the parable teaches that God will not make the final separation in this age. Some used it to reject all church discipline, but Matthew 18 and 1 Corinthians 5 call for discipline; the parable warns against trying to judge hearts as only God can. It also warns that not everyone who says "Lord, Lord" will enter; like a counterfeit bill, pretenders will be exposed.

sa.prompt: Explain the parable of the mustard seed, including the interpretive views and the connection to faith.
sa.model: The mustard seed was the proverbially smallest seed, yet black mustard grew taller than a man; Jesus was not teaching botany. Birds nesting in a great tree echo Old Testament images of a kingdom sheltering the nations, so most read it as a promise of astonishing growth from small beginnings. Some older dispensational teachers saw the birds as evil and the growth as corruption. Jesus also spoke of faith as a mustard seed; small real faith grows.

sa.prompt: Explain the parables of the hidden treasure and the pearl and how they contrast with the rich young ruler.
sa.model: A man found treasure hidden in a field and for joy sold all he had to buy it; a merchant found one pearl of great price and sold all to buy it. One found the kingdom by surprise and one after a long search, but both gave everything with joy. The rich young ruler would not sell what he had and went away sad. The kingdom costs everything and is worth far more than it costs.

sa.prompt: Explain the setting of Matthew 13 and the questions its kingdom parables answer.
sa.model: Matthew 13 gathers seven kingdom parables, beginning with the sower, right after the religious leaders accused Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebub; from then He taught the crowds in parables. They answer why evil still grows alongside good, why the kingdom looks so small, and whether it is worth the cost. The kingdom grows mixed with evil until the harvest, begins small but becomes great, and is worth everything we have.

sa.prompt: Explain the parable of the leaven, including the interpretive debate and its lesson.
sa.model: A woman hid leaven, a piece of fermented dough, in three measures of meal, about fifty pounds, the same amount Sarah baked, until all was leavened. Elsewhere leaven often pictures sin, as in the leaven of the Pharisees, so a few read this as corruption spreading. Most note that Jesus says the kingdom is like leaven and pairs it with the mustard seed, so it teaches that the kingdom works quietly from the inside out until it transforms everything.

sa.prompt: Explain the parables of the dragnet and the householder and what each teaches.
sa.model: A dragnet gathers fish of every kind, and only on the shore are the good sorted from the bad; Jesus explains this pictures the end of the age when angels separate the wicked from the just, so our task is to cast the net wide. The householder brings out of his treasure things new and old, a picture of the teacher of the kingdom, and especially the preacher, who serves both the Old Testament and Christ's teaching.

sa.prompt: Explain how tares can appear in the church and in the heart, using the talk-show woman, the woman at the well, and lending money.
sa.model: A talk-show guest having an affair said she was a Christian but her religion had nothing to do with her personal life, because God wanted her happy; tares can speak the language of wheat. Yet in the woman at the well, whose life seemed hopeless, Jesus saw a longing for living water like wheat among weeds. Only God sees the heart; years of lending to strangers show our judgment is poor. Tares may even look better than wheat, but they make poor bread.

sa.prompt: Discuss the ethical question and the alternative interpretation raised by the treasure and pearl, and explain Jim Elliot's words.
sa.model: Some ask whether the man acted honestly by buying the field without revealing the treasure; the parable uses an everyday situation to make one point, not to teach real estate ethics: something of infinite worth is worth giving up everything. Some read the pearl merchant as Christ buying His church, a true doctrine, but most see the one who finds the kingdom. Jim Elliot wrote, "He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose."

sa.prompt: Outline how a pastor might preach a series from the kingdom parables of Matthew 13.
sa.model: Preach the wheat and tares in movements, the sowing, the growing together, and the harvest, closing with the question, "Am I wheat?" and Romans 10:13. Pair the mustard seed and leaven as encouragement for small churches, showing outward growth and inward power. Preach the treasure and pearl as total commitment with joy beside the rich young ruler. Close with the dragnet's certainty of final judgment and the urgency of casting the net.
